passage: Sunday night. Recital tomorrow!! My hands are shaking a little and my mouth feels dry like chalk. Leela Ma'am said it is nerves and excitement mixed together, they feel the same in the body. She showed me to breathe in for four counts and out slowly, so I did it three times. It helped a bit. Then I played the whole Raag once for Amma, who sat there like a rock and smiled at the end. I still feel butterflies but they're smaller. I'll wear my blue kurta and look at Amma when I begin. If I mess up I will just go on. 🙂 — Chetan

qa.q: What colour kurta will Chetan wear to the recital?
qa.a: Chetan will wear a blue kurta.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel the night before the recital, and how could the shaking hands be read differently?
qa.a: Chetan felt nervous, with shaky hands and a dry mouth, and also excited. Leela Ma'am said the two feelings feel the same in the body.

qa.q: What could Chetan do on the recital day to help himself settle?
qa.a: Chetan could breathe slowly as practised, look at Amma at the start, and keep going after any mistake.

qa.q: How does playing for Amma help Chetan?
qa.a: Amma sits still and smiles at the end, giving Chetan a familiar friendly face and the confidence that the piece is fine.

grounding: A child before a recital shows shaking hands and a dry mouth, which reflect nervous excitement, and settles through slow breathing, rehearsal and a familiar face.

passage: At the temple fair in Anandpur, Kiran waited behind the curtain of the makeshift stage, holding her flute. Her hands trembled and her mouth was so dry that she took a sip from her steel glass. Her uncle Baljeet, who ran the sound system, crouched beside her. "Breathe in slowly," he said, "like smelling a flower. Out like blowing on hot chai." She did it three times. "Do you see Nani in the front row?" he asked. She peeked through the gap and Nani gave her a thumbs-up. Kiran's shoulders lowered a little. When her name was called she walked on, took a big breath, and began to play.

qa.q: Where did Kiran wait before her turn?
qa.a: She waited behind the curtain of the makeshift stage at the temple fair in Anandpur.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's hands tremble, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: She was probably nervous about performing, but the trembling can also be excitement. Her calmer shoulders after seeing Nani suggest fear was part of it.

qa.q: What could Kiran do if her nerves return before another performance?
qa.a: She could breathe slowly, look for a friendly face in the crowd, and rehearse the tune beforehand, as she and Baljeet did.

qa.q: How does Baljeet's help affect Kiran?
qa.a: Baljeet stays calm and gives simple breathing images, so Kiran does not feel alone. Seeing Nani helps her body settle.

grounding: A child before a recital shows shaking hands and a dry voice, and slow breathing and a friendly face help her settle.

passage:
Backstage at the music school in Seoul, Soo-ah's hands would not stop shaking. She pressed them between her knees. Her mouth felt as dry as paper, and the piano in the hall looked a mile away.
"Is it fear or excitement?" her teacher asked quietly. Soo-ah couldn't tell. Her heart was racing either way.
"Breathe with me. In for four, out for six." They did it three times. Her shoulders dropped a little.
When her name was called, she walked out and searched the rows. There was Abebe from her class, in the third row, giving a tiny thumbs-up.
Soo-ah sat, placed her fingers on the keys the way she had practised a hundred times, and began. The first notes wobbled. By the fourth line, her hands were steady.

qa.q: Where was Abebe sitting?
qa.a: In the third row.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's shaking and dry mouth suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Soo-ah was most likely nervous, but the racing heart could just as well be excitement; even she could not tell which, as her teacher's question shows.

qa.q: Which things helped Soo-ah's body settle?
qa.a: Slow breathing with her teacher, the piece she had practised many times, and spotting Abebe's friendly face all helped her hands grow steady.

qa.q: What is it like for Abebe watching from the third row?
qa.a: Abebe may feel a little nervous for Soo-ah and eager to help, which is why the tiny thumbs-up matters.

grounding: Before a recital, a child's shaking hands and dry mouth show nervous excitement, and breathing, rehearsal and a friendly face help her settle.

passage:
At the community centre's inter-school singing contest, Lokesh sat in the green room, sipping water again and again. His voice cracked when he tried a warm-up note.
"My throat's gone," he croaked. "I can't."
Vishal, the centre's music volunteer, pulled a chair close. "Hands on your belly. Breathe so your hands move, not your shoulders." Lokesh tried. Slow in, slower out.
"Now hum the first line. Just hum."
The hum came out wobbly, then smoother. Vishal grinned. "You've sung this at every practice for a month. Your voice knows it even when your brain panics."
On stage, Lokesh found Vishal at the side and kept glancing at him. His first note was thin, but by the chorus it filled the room.

qa.q: What did Vishal ask Lokesh to hum?
qa.a: The first line.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh say "I can't"?
qa.a: Lokesh felt panicky and scared because his voice cracked, and he believed his throat had gone; the dry voice may also have been nervous excitement before a big moment.

qa.q: What steps did Vishal use to calm Lokesh?
qa.a: Vishal guided belly breathing, then a gentle hum, and reminded Lokesh of a month of practice, which settled the body before singing.

qa.q: How might Vishal see the cracked voice in the green room?
qa.a: Vishal seems to see it as normal pre-stage nerves rather than a real problem, which is why the volunteer stays calm and practical.

grounding: A child's dry, cracking voice before a contest settles with slow breathing, reminders of rehearsal and a familiar face.

passage:
I sat next to Zainab in the waiting row before the school's recitation contest. She kept rubbing her palms on her kurta and whispering her lines. When the teacher called the name before hers, her knee started bouncing so fast the bench shook.
I couldn't tell if she was scared or just excited; she was also half-smiling.
She closed her eyes and took three long breaths, slow ones, the kind our PT sir teaches. Then she looked around until she found her Ammi in the back row, waving a dupatta end.
When Zainab went up, her first words were a bit soft. Then her voice grew clear.
After, she told me her hands had been ice-cold. I told her I couldn't see that from outside.
- Gargi

qa.q: Who did Zainab find in the back row?
qa.a: Her Ammi, waving a dupatta end.

qa.q: What might Zainab have been feeling while her knee bounced?
qa.a: She was probably nervous, but the half-smile hints she may also have felt excited; Gargi, watching, could not be sure which.

qa.q: What helped Zainab settle before going up?
qa.a: Taking slow breaths and finding her Ammi's familiar face in the crowd helped her body calm down.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Zainab's nerves compared with how Zainab felt?
qa.a: From outside Gargi mostly saw a bouncing knee and then a clear voice, while inside Zainab felt ice-cold hands, so nerves can be bigger inside than they look.

grounding: An observer watches a child's nervous signs before a recitation and how breathing and a familiar face help her settle.

passage:
Ten days before: At veena class, Arohi's fingers slipped on the strings every time Swati Aunty said, "Now imagine the audience." Swati Aunty showed her a slow breath in through the nose and a longer one out, and they played the piece again and again until it felt boring.
Recital day: Arohi's mouth was dry and her hands trembled on the wooden neck. Was it fear or excitement? Maybe both. She breathed the slow way twice, found Meher's face in the third row, and Meher wiggled her eyebrows. Arohi began. The first note wobbled; the second didn't.
The next morning: Arohi told Swati Aunty, "My hands shook the whole first line, but they still knew the way." Swati Aunty smiled. "That's what the boring practice was for."

qa.q: What instrument does Arohi play?
qa.a: The veena.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on recital day when her hands trembled?
qa.a: Arohi felt a mix of fear and excitement, with a dry mouth and trembling hands, and wasn't sure which feeling it was.

qa.q: Which tools helped Arohi's body settle?
qa.a: The slow breath, practising until the piece felt boring, and finding Meher's friendly face in the audience.

qa.q: What would change if Arohi had skipped the boring practice?
qa.a: Her hands would have had no well-worn path to follow, so the shaking could have taken over the whole piece.

grounding: It illustrates a child's shaking hands and dry mouth before a recital as nervous excitement, settled by slow breathing, rehearsal and a familiar face.
